title: A little nudge goes a long way
author: Ben Rice
summary: Ben Rice tells the story of transforming his History department's after-school revision sessions from a poorly-attended fixture (fewer than 15 students a week) into a session that drew 73 students, and uses it to make a simple claim about student motivation: the intervention that worked was not a new incentive scheme, a bribe, or a parent-contact campaign, but individually and warmly asking each student, by name, whether they were coming. He is explicit that the piece is not an argument for or against compulsory after-school revision, nor a guide to running an effective session -- it's narrowly about what got students in the room. Rice describes the mechanics: personal, low-pressure invitations delivered in corridors and at the end of lessons, spoken warmly rather than as a demand, sometimes reinforced by peer social pressure when students called each other out for lying about conflicts. He frames the tactic as costless -- it didn't add to his workload because he was talking to these students anyway -- and connects it to a broader point about care: the personal ask signals to students that a teacher is invested in them specifically, which he argues is what actually moved the needle where impersonal reminders (letters, blanket announcements) had not.
points: Central finding: personally and individually asking each student to attend, rather than relying on blanket announcements, letters, or bribes, took attendance from under 15 to 73 students at an after-school revision session.
Frames the tactic as low-cost/no-cost: because Rice was already talking to these students informally around the school, the individual asks didn't add measurable workload.

Distinguishes the intervention's mechanism from typical incentive-based strategies (food, praise, parent calls), arguing that the personal, warm ask signals specific care in a way generic incentives don't.
Notes that peer social pressure amplified the personal asks once other students started calling out reluctant classmates directly, showing how individual outreach can cascade into group norms.

Anchors the account in delayed-payoff evidence: a student who initially attended reluctantly returned after the real exam specifically to credit the extra session with saving him on a high-mark question.
quotes: [1] "So what did our team do? When colleagues in other departments asked what wizardry we'd conjured up, my answer disappointed them- 'we simply asked them'. Individually.

[2] "Like many teachers, I had tried the usual strategies: calling parents, sending letters, praising attendees, holding back students after lessons. I even attempted to bribe students with food. Each tactic occasionally nudged a student, but not significant numbers.

[3] "'Alright Sam, tell me about Ancoats in the 20th Century? You can't? But that's 100% coming up in the exam, I'd hate for you to miss those marks. 20 minutes, that you'll definitely need Sam!' I always said it warmly and with a smile, never confrontational.

[4] "It didn't add to my workload- I'd have spoken to these students around school anyways, out of politeness. It just became a thing I did... I like to think it showed the students I really cared about them, wanted the best for them.

[5] "Oh, and the student I mentioned earlier who thanked me- he came up after the real exam with a glint in his eyes: 'Lucky I went to that session earlier in the year, sir, or I'd have been stuffed in the 16-marker.'
